claims.text: Adding a minor amount of aluminum to steels designed for chemical-processing and nuclear applications enhances their corrosion resistance.
The corrosion-resistance enhancement is governed by formation and maintenance of a continuous chromium-rich passive layer.
Aluminum undergoes preferential oxidation or dissolution and acts as a sacrificial element.
Dissolved aluminum forms AlCl3 and establishes an Al/AlCl3 redox couple in chloride environments.
The Al/AlCl3 redox couple buffers the local electrochemical potential.
Sacrificial aluminum dissolution reduces the rate of chromium dissolution or depletion from the alloy.
Preserving chromium in the surface layer sustains passivation and corrosion protection.
Protective aluminum oxide or chloride species assist formation or maintenance of the chromium-rich passive film.
Aluminum-containing steel will develop thinner or non-propagating chromium-depletion zones than an otherwise identical aluminum-free steel.
Aluminum-containing steel will have a lower overall corrosion rate than an otherwise identical aluminum-free steel.
The proposed mechanism should operate in molten chloride salts at elevated temperatures.
The proposed mechanism should also operate in aqueous, high-chloride chemical-processing environments.
Chromium is the main passivating element in the target steels.
Chromium is particularly vulnerable to dissolution during molten-salt corrosion of nuclear structural alloys.
The aluminum concentration must be optimized to avoid deleterious effects on mechanical properties.
The magnitude of protection may depend on alloy composition, microstructure, and the precise corrosive environment.
Grain-boundary diffusion in ultrafine-grained steels may provide an additional diffusion-driven corrosion-resistance enhancement.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both chromium-depletion depth and corrosion rate relative to the aluminum-free control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
